mnemonic: คะ and ค่ะ are the same soft syllable from the same woman; only the pitch differs. ค่ะ drops, and that is a full stop. คะ stays up high and holds the sentence open, because a question cannot end flat. The pitch is the question mark. (▲ high and taut, the sentence left hanging)
scene: A shopkeeper in her doorway leaning slightly towards a customer, one eyebrow lifted, chin raised, palm open in a polite enquiring gesture. Beside her a second woman stands square and settled, hands folded, head level. Warm afternoon light through the open shopfront.

mnemonic: A traffic cop hands back the wallet you dropped, and the thanks is already built into the word: คุณ khun means you, so khàawp-khun is thanks-you, and the cop is standing right there to collect it. Palms together, head down, the first syllable sitting low. (▁ khàawp drops low, then khun levels out flat and mid)
scene: A Bangkok street corner in the rain. A traffic policeman in a white helmet holds out a battered leather wallet to a young woman, who has stopped mid-step and pressed her palms together in front of her face, head bowed, beaming.

mnemonic: The same "my?" as ไหม — but shouted across a noisy bar, so the voice snaps up high and stays there instead of gliding. มั้ย is what friends say; ไหม is its polite written twin. (▲ high and flat-topped, a quick shout)
scene: Crowded noisy Thai bar at night, packed with people. In the foreground a young man leans over a table, hands cupped around his mouth, shouting across the room toward a friend. The friend at the far side cups a hand behind his ear, squinting to hear.

mnemonic: The contract is signed, everyone is smiling — but then the lawyer tears the last page clean off. Tɛ̀ɛ is that tear: everything before it stands, and what comes after changes it. Say it like 'tear' with the R swallowed. (▁ low and flat, the paper comes away without drama)
scene: A boardroom. A lawyer stands at the head of the table calmly ripping the bottom sheet off a stapled contract, the torn strip already curling. Three people around the table, smiles frozen, one half out of a chair.

mnemonic: She asks for chilli and the cook reaches for the whole jar. "Nòi!" — voice dropping low as she pinches her fingers a centimetre apart. Just a bit. (▁ low and small, the voice shrinks with the gesture)
scene: A street food stall. The cook, grinning, is tipping an enormous jar of dried red chilli flakes toward a bowl of noodles. Across the counter a woman lunges forward with one hand raised in alarm, her other hand pinching thumb and forefinger a tiny distance apart.

mnemonic: The foreman watches the machine cough into life, sticks his thumb up, and the whole line starts moving. Tham is the doing word — make, do, get it done — and whatever the job is, the thumb settles it. (— flat and level, no fuss in it)
scene: A factory floor. A foreman in a hard hat stands beside a starting conveyor with his thumb raised toward a control booth above. Workers along the line reach for the first parts coming through. Cold overhead lighting, oil-stained concrete.

mnemonic: He cannot get the sentence out, so he puts the words down one at a time like stones across a stream until they reach the far bank. Say put with a long oo: phûut, to speak. (↓ falling, each word dropped into place)
scene: A man crouched at the edge of a shallow stream placing flat stepping stones into the water one by one, a line of them already reaching halfway across to a woman waiting on the far bank. Morning mist, reeds, soft grey light.

mnemonic: The stall keeps the same leaves and pours a third round from them, because nothing here is finished until it cannot be used again. Chái is to use — to put a thing to work. (▲ high and taut, a brisk working word)
scene: A roadside tea stall. A vendor pours from a battered dented pot into a glass, the spent leaves heaped in a strainer beside her, three used glasses waiting. Close crop on hands and steam, sunlit street beyond.

mnemonic: A boy snatches a roasting chestnut straight off the brazier — ow — and hangs on to it anyway, because he wants it. Ao is wanting and taking in one syllable, and the vendor will throw it at you as a question. (— flat and level, said fast)
scene: A street brazier of chestnuts glowing over coals. A small boy has just grabbed one and is shaking his hand in the air, chestnut clamped in his fingers, face screwed up. The vendor leans back laughing. Night, sparks, orange light.

mnemonic: Every cake on the stand sits on its own lace doily, and each doily was cut by hand by the woman behind the counter — made by her. Dooi is the by-word: done by, through, by means of. (— flat and level, a quiet credit)
scene: A glass-fronted cake stand. A woman's hands lower a small iced cake onto a white lace doily on the top shelf, a stack of cut doilies beside her. Scissors and paper scraps on the counter. Bright shop light.

mnemonic: You suggest something ridiculous. Your friend shakes her head once and sets a heavy rock down on the table between you. Solid as a rock: no, definitely not, don't even think it. (▁ low and flat, the last word on the matter)
scene: Two friends at a small café table. One leans forward mid-sentence, hands open, pleading. The other has just set a heavy grey river stone down on the tabletop between them with a thud, and is shaking her head once, eyebrows raised, utterly unmoved. Coffee cups rattle slightly.

mnemonic: A rented room in a Hong Kong tower block, so small that a man standing in the middle of it reaches both walls without straightening his arms. Hong, hâawng: the room. This one is all the room there is, and the voice drops like the ceiling. (↓ falling, heavy and low)
scene: A tiny high-rise flat. A man stands in the centre with both arms half raised, palms flat against opposite walls, a folded bed and a single hotplate crammed in behind him.

mnemonic: Asked whether the mangoes will be ripe by Friday, the farmer looks up at the tree, tips his hand from side to side and says máng — probably, don't hold me to it. The first syllable of mango, thrown up high. (▲ high, the voice lifts and leaves it open)
scene: A mango orchard. A farmer stands under a heavy tree of half-ripe fruit, one hand tipping side to side at chest height, squinting up. A buyer beside him with an empty crate waits. Hot hazy light through leaves.

mnemonic: The first tray out of the oven goes onto the top rack, too hot to touch, while the window is still dark. Stretch it — raaack — and you have rɛ̂ɛk: the first one, the first time. (↓ falling, the tray lands)
scene: A bakery before dawn. A baker slides a tray of pale rolls onto the top shelf of a tall steel cooling rack, every shelf below it empty. Dark window, flour dust in the lamplight.

mnemonic: Ask for a different room and the clerk turns to the board of hanging keys for another one. Say 'oon' with the lips spread flat, not pushed forward, and you have ɯ̀ɯn: the other one, some other, a different one from this. (▁ low and flat, a plain alternative)
scene: A small hotel desk. A clerk reaches up to a board of keys hanging on hooks, one hand on a key, while a guest waits with a bag at her feet.

mnemonic: He gets to the buffet one minute late and the tray is already gone. He should have come before. Gɔ̀ɔn is before, first, ahead of the other thing. (▁ low and flat, the word lands after the fact)
scene: A function hall after the rush. A man in a suit stares down at an empty steel serving tray with tongs lying across it, crumbs and a smear of sauce left. Stacked chairs, other emptied trays, cold strip lighting.

mnemonic: The fridge dies in the night and the whole tray of prawns has turned. She holds one up at arm's length, pulls a face and drops it in the bin: see-ya. Sǐa is spoiled, wasted, broken, gone bad. (↑ rising, the voice lifts on the last of it)
scene: A kitchen at night lit only by an open fridge. A woman holds a prawn at arm's length over a bin with her face turned away, a tray of them on the counter beside her. Harsh white fridge light, dark room.

mnemonic: A crow on the café railing caws at every table in turn until somebody gives up a chip. Kʰɔ̌ɔ is asking for — a favour, a discount, one more minute — and the voice climbs the way the caw does. (↑ rising, the call lifts at the end)
scene: A seaside café terrace. A crow perched on the railing leans toward a table of chips with its beak open, wings half lifted, while two diners shield their plates with their forearms. Bright overcast light, gulls beyond.

mnemonic: The word kept for a judge, a monk or a minister — closer to 'sir' than to 'you'. It sounds like the 'than' in thank you, and thanking is about the right register: the clerk bows before every sentence. (↓ falling, the head dips with the voice)
scene: A panelled antechamber. A young clerk bows from the waist as he holds out a closed file with both hands to a robed elder who is reaching for it. Dark wood, brass lamp, one high window.

mnemonic: The magician slaps the table — dang — and whips the cloth away to show what was underneath it all along. Sà-dɛɛng is to show, to display, to perform. (— the second syllable holds flat and level, the reveal)
scene: A small stage. A magician sweeps a red cloth up and off a table, a brass birdcage revealed beneath it mid-flourish, the cloth still in the air. Footlights, dark auditorium, a few faces in the front row.

mnemonic: A boy at the paint counter prises the lid off one tin after another to see what is actually inside each one, because colour is the thing you can only know by looking. Sǐi is colour, and it sounds exactly like 'see'. (↑ rising, the lid comes up)
scene: A hardware shop paint counter. A boy levers the lid off a tin of bright blue paint with a screwdriver, a row of already-opened tins of different colours beside him, lids stacked. Bright shop light.

mnemonic: Dawn in a camp: the cook bangs a ladle on the pot and the whole sleepy line shuffles up for chow. Breakfast is the first thing that happens in a Thai morning, and cháaw is the morning itself. (▲ high and bright, a shout across a cold yard)
scene: Dawn in a field camp. A cook in an apron ladles steaming rice porridge into the tin bowls of a queue of sleepy workers, their breath showing in the cold.

mnemonic: Nah — the tea is not ready, it wants another minute. naa-thii is that gap exactly: the sand running through while the leaves open and nobody does anything useful. Nah, tea. Sixty seconds and not a second less. (— both syllables flat, the way a minute just sits there)
scene: A kitchen counter in morning light. A squat teapot steams beside a small hourglass timer, its sand halfway run through.

mnemonic: The fairground strongman brings the mallet down and the puck goes all the way up the tower: the bell at the top rang, and rang loud enough to stop the music. แรง is that. Force, power, the strength that made the bell speak. (— flat and level, held like a struck note)
scene: A night fairground high striker. A heavily built man in a vest has just swung a mallet onto the pad, the puck streaking up the tower, and the brass bell at the top is jolting sideways mid-strike.

mnemonic: He ducks under the table after a dropped coin and comes up short — his tie is pinned beneath the table leg and his neck will go no further. Under the table is where the tie is, and where he now lives. tâi. (↓ falling, the word drops with him)
scene: A man in a suit on hands and knees half beneath a dining table, neck yanked sideways because his necktie is trapped under a table leg, a dropped coin just past his fingertips. Low view, warm light.

mnemonic: On the museum shelf the heart comes first and the lung in the jar comes after it, always after, never before. Lung, jar: lǎng-jàak. Hear the lid click shut on the end of jàak, and remember that หลัง on its own means behind. (↑ lǎng climbs, then jàak drops low and clipped)
scene: A dim museum shelf of specimen jars. A curator's gloved hand rests on the second jar, which holds a pale lung suspended in fluid; the first jar beside it holds a heart.

mnemonic: Knock the O off TANGO and you have tɛ̀ng. Nobody dances a tango in their work clothes: the word is getting dressed, arranged, put together properly. The same verb composes a song — cloth or music, it is all arranging. (▁ low and flat, the pause before the music starts)
scene: A dressing room doorway. A woman in a fitted scarlet dance dress stands with arms raised while an older dresser kneels to pin her hem; beside her a man in a black suit adjusts his cuffs.

mnemonic: She walks the line of her class the way a captain walks the deck in front of a crew — khruu, crew, the one who keeps the whole lot upright and moving in the same direction. One flat syllable, said with respect. (— flat and level, unhurried)
scene: A sunlit Thai schoolyard. A teacher in a neat uniform walks slowly along a line of pupils standing to attention, hands clasped behind her back, inspecting them; the children stand straight-backed, one sneaking a grin. Dusty ground, green trees, hard morning light.

mnemonic: The herd files into the milking shed and the farmer counts them through the gate. The ninth cow is always the one that stops in the doorway to think about it, and the gate comes down behind her. Nine cows: gâo. (↓ falling, the gate drops)
scene: A milking shed doorway at dusk. Eight cows are already inside the lit shed; the ninth stands square in the open gateway, head turned back, refusing to move. A farmer leans on the gatepost with one hand raised mid-count.

mnemonic: She sings one last la— down the platform and then she is gone. laa-gɔ̀ɔn: a la, and gone. It is the goodbye for someone leaving properly, not the see-you-tomorrow kind. (▁ gɔ̀ɔn drops low, the sound of a door pulled shut)
scene: A railway platform at dusk. A woman leans out of the window of a moving carriage with one arm raised in a wave, mouth open mid-note; on the emptying platform a man watches the train shrink away.

mnemonic: The old carpenter lays his hands over the boy's on the saw and pushes, pulls, pushes, until the plank is sawn through. He does not cut it for him. sǎawn is that: teaching, passing the thing on. (↑ rising, the voice climbs like the saw coming back up)
scene: A dusty workshop. An old carpenter stands behind a boy at a sawhorse with his weathered hands laid over the boy's on the saw handle, a plank half cut through beneath them, curls of sawdust drifting in a shaft of light from a grimy window.

mnemonic: The same chow as cháaw, morning — but let the voice fall instead of holding it up high and the meaning changes to rent. The morning goes up; the rent comes down, out of your hand and into the landlady's. (↓ falling, the voice drops as the notes leave your fingers)
scene: A shophouse doorway at dusk. A young tenant counts banknotes one by one into the open palm of an elderly landlady, who holds a ring of keys in her other hand.

mnemonic: Tick, and on the tock the coconut lets go. It is a hand's width above the dust now, directly over a man who has slept through the whole business. ตก is anything that falls: rain, prices, a man off a ladder. (▁ low and short, the sound of the landing)
scene: Beneath a coconut palm at noon. A large green coconut hangs frozen in the air a hand's width above the dusty ground, right beside a man dozing against the trunk with his hat over his face. A cat is already leaping clear.

mnemonic: Four men are hammering at a coconut and getting nowhere. The cook walks over, turns it in her palm and opens it with one tap of the cleaver's spine. That is the witty way: wí-thii, the method. A hard t in the middle, never an English th. (— the second syllable holds flat and long, wi-THEE)
scene: An outdoor kitchen. Four men crouch over a coconut with hammers and a rock, husk fibres scattered everywhere. Beside them a small woman in an apron holds a coconut in one palm, the spine of her cleaver tapping its middle, the shell already opening cleanly in two.

mnemonic: พ่อ is PAW, the father, with a round aw in the middle. พา is PAH, with an open ah, and it means to take someone along with you. Here the pa does both: his hand closes round the child's wrist and he tows her through the crowd without breaking stride. (— flat and level, the pace never changes)
scene: A packed night market seen from behind. A tall father in a work shirt cuts through the crowd with a small girl's wrist held firmly in his hand, her feet skipping to keep up, her free hand clutching a skewer.

mnemonic: A geologist lifts a long core out of the ground under an enormous moon, and everything about the place is there in its bands. kʰɔ̂ɔ is a single item, muun is the raw stuff: core and moon together, kʰɔ̂ɔ-muun, the information. (↓ falls on kʰɔ̂ɔ, then muun levels out flat)
scene: Night in an open field. A geologist crouches holding up a long cylindrical soil core banded in coloured layers, turning it in gloved hands under the beam of a head torch.
